steps.label: OPEN
steps.title: 30 people. One experiment.
steps.lead: Today you will build, test, challenge, and revise a model of how AI works.
steps.instructorCue: Welcome students, get everyone connected, and frame the room as one shared experiment.

steps.label: RETRIEVE
steps.title: What would an AI need to know before you trusted this answer?
steps.lead: You ask an AI system: “Should I drop my calculus course?” Name one piece of information it would need.
steps.placeholder: One thing the AI would need to know is…
steps.instructorCue: Give 60–90 seconds of quiet thinking. Spotlight two contrasting responses.

steps.label: TEACH
steps.title: Separate the system into five parts.
steps.lead: This lens will help us reason about almost any AI-supported decision.
steps.instructorCue: Teach the five-part lens with a familiar example before returning to the advising case.

steps.label: DO
steps.title: Build the advising system.
steps.lead: Describe what belongs in each part of the calculus-advice system.
steps.instructorCue: Students work individually first, then compare with a neighbor. Ask what they disagree about.

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.title: Should the AI recommend dropping the course?
steps.lead: Known information: GPA 2.8 · Calculus grade D · Major: Computer Science
steps.instructorCue: Lock responses after most students vote. Do not reveal immediately.

steps.label: REVEAL + DISCUSS
steps.title: The class has committed.
steps.lead: Now look at the system, not just the answer.
steps.prompt: What assumptions are hiding behind these recommendations?
steps.instructorCue: Reveal the distribution. Ask students to defend the least popular answer before discussing assumptions.

steps.label: UPDATE
steps.title: New information. Does your recommendation change?
steps.lead: Calculus is a prerequisite for three courses the student planned to take next semester.
steps.instructorCue: Ask students to vote again without discussion first, then notice who changed positions.

steps.label: DISCUSS
steps.title: The information changed. So did the problem.
steps.lead: What does the shift tell us about data, models, and human judgment?
steps.hero: The model did not become “more intelligent.” The information available to the decision changed.
steps.instructorCue: Connect the class shift explicitly to data quality, context, and decision consequences.

steps.label: FAILURE TEST
steps.title: Where can this system fail?
steps.lead: Choose the point you think creates the greatest risk.
choices: MODEL / TOOL: bad assumptions or patterns
steps.instructorCue: Use the distribution to show that responsible AI is a system problem, not only a model problem.

steps.label: THINK
steps.title: What is still the human’s job?
steps.lead: Complete the sentence in one strong thought.
steps.placeholder: Even with AI support, a human still needs to…
steps.instructorCue: Spotlight two strong responses and connect them to human responsibility.

steps.label: EXIT + CLOSE
steps.title: What changed in your thinking today?
steps.lead: Write one thing you understand differently now about how AI systems work.
steps.placeholder: Before today I thought… Now I think…
steps.closing: AI can support a decision. It does not remove responsibility.
steps.instructorCue: Collect the exit signal, restate the five-part lens, and close exactly at 75 minutes.
